title: First case of West Nile virus in NC found in Durham County patient, NCDHHS says - NewsBreak
text: DURHAM, N.C. (WNCN) — The first case of West Nile virus in the state of North Carolina in 2025 has been reported, according to the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services. The person infected by the mosquito-borne disease is a resident of Durham County, the state health department said. According to Durham County officials, it is the first case of West Nile there since 2022. No other information about the patient, including how old they are or where they were possibly infected, is being released to protect their privacy, both the state and county said. NCDHHS said routine monitoring in Pitt County has also identified “West Nile virus-infected mosquitoes” in that county. “This is the time of year when West Nile virus activity typically increases across North Carolina,” Emily Herring, NCDHHS Public Health Veterinarian, said in a release. “This recent case highlights the importance of preventing mosquito bites to reduce the risk of infection.” The virus doesn’t always produce symptoms — in fact, public health officials said most people who are infected with West Nile won’t experience any. But those who do will develop a fever as well as other symptoms such as body aches, joint pain and a headache. Of those infected, about one in 150 will develop “a serious neurologic illness” that presents itself in symptoms like high fever, neck stiffness, disorientation and even seizures and paralysis. In North Carolina, it is only these cases of neurologic illness associated with West Nile virus that are reportable, public health officials said. Though not all mosquitoes carry West Nile, the types that “that most commonly transmit the virus can be found statewide and are most active between dusk and dawn,” according to NCDHHS. Public health officials at all levels are encouraging prevention of not just mosquito-borne viruses like West Nile, but also others that can be carried by various small bugs. “The best way to prevent West Nile virus is to prevent any mosquito bites, especially this time of year when mosquito activity is higher,” said Durham County Department of Public Health Environmental Health Director James Salter in a release. “People should take steps to prevent mosquito bites and all bug bites anytime they’re going to be outside in order to reduce their risk of getting West Nile or any vector-borne diseases, which are diseases carried by mosquitoes, fleas, and ticks.” For the latest news, weather, sports, and streaming video, head to Queen City News.
